title: Monoclonal Protein: MGUS or Multiple Myeloma?
bottomLine: An incidental monoclonal protein is not automatically myeloma, but anemia, renal dysfunction, hypercalcemia, bone pain, lytic lesions or other myeloma-defining features require prompt hematology assessment.
recognize: Myeloma can present with fractures, back pain, recurrent infections, anemia or kidney injury.
differentiate: MGUS lacks myeloma-defining organ damage and has lower clonal burden, but still requires risk-based follow-up.
assessment: Ask about bone pain, fractures, infection, neuropathy, weight loss and renal symptoms.
workup: Use CBC, calcium, creatinine, serum and urine monoclonal protein studies and free light chains, with imaging and marrow evaluation under hematology when indicated.
management: Refer suspected myeloma promptly; MGUS follow-up depends on risk category.
medicationSafety: NSAIDs and dehydration can worsen kidney injury in plasma-cell disease.
counselling: Explain that MGUS is not cancer but is monitored because a minority of cases progress.
examTrap: Reassuring an older adult with a monoclonal protein plus new anemia or kidney dysfunction that it is merely MGUS.
oneLinePearl: Monoclonal protein plus organ damage is not benign until proven otherwise.
sourceBasis: Myeloma Canada and Canadian hematology practice resources

title: Oncologic Emergencies: The Cancer Diagnosis Does Not Explain Everything
bottomLine: Cancer patients with acute deterioration require rapid recognition of spinal cord compression, superior vena cava syndrome, tumor lysis, hypercalcemia, neutropenic sepsis and treatment complications. New symptoms should not be dismissed as expected cancer burden.
recognize: Back pain with weakness suggests cord compression; facial or upper-extremity swelling suggests SVC obstruction; electrolyte derangement after therapy can signal tumor lysis.
differentiate: Opioid toxicity, pulmonary embolism, infection and metabolic disease commonly coexist with cancer.
assessment: Assess ABCs, neurologic deficits, treatment timing, cancer type and stage, fever, volume status and current antineoplastic agents.
workup: Use syndrome-specific urgent MRI or CT, CBC, electrolytes, uric acid, calcium, renal function and cultures.
management: Stabilize and activate oncology or critical-care pathways; treat cord compression, sepsis, tumor lysis and severe hypercalcemia immediately.
medicationSafety: Cancer therapies have specific cardiotoxic, immunologic, thrombotic and infection risks; medication reconciliation must include oral and infused agents.
counselling: Give treatment-specific emergency symptoms before patients leave oncology care.
followUp: Ensure acute-care handoff to oncology includes therapies held or restarted and all pending results.
examTrap: Assuming severe new back pain in a patient with cancer is ordinary musculoskeletal pain without a neurologic examination.
oneLinePearl: Cancer changes the emergency differential; it does not eliminate it.

title: Anticoagulant Bleeding: Severity, Drug, Timing, Reversal
bottomLine: Major bleeding on anticoagulation requires rapid stabilization, identification of the anticoagulant and last dose, renal function, bleeding site and cause-specific reversal. Minor bleeding does not justify automatic permanent discontinuation.
recognize: Critical-site bleeding, hemodynamic compromise, significant hemoglobin drop or transfusion need defines major bleeding clinically.
differentiate: DOAC effect is not reliably measured by INR; warfarin reversal differs from factor-Xa or dabigatran reversal.
assessment: Assess ABCs, bleeding source, last dose, renal function, interacting drugs, antiplatelets and the indication for anticoagulation.
workup: Use CBC, drug-appropriate coagulation testing, renal function, type and crossmatch and source-directed imaging or endoscopy.
management: Hold anticoagulant, control the source and use specific or nonspecific reversal according to agent and severity; restart decisions balance thrombosis and rebleeding.
medicationSafety: Vitamin K reverses warfarin but not DOACs; PCC and specific antidotes have agent-specific roles.
counselling: After stabilization, review NSAIDs, alcohol, duplicate antiplatelets and adherence.
followUp: Document when and why anticoagulation is restarted or permanently stopped.
examTrap: Using INR to decide whether apixaban has clinically important anticoagulant effect.
oneLinePearl: Bleeding reversal starts by naming the anticoagulant and the last dose.
sourceBasis: Thrombosis Canada DOAC bleeding and warfarin clinical guides

title: Cancer-Associated VTE: Clot and Bleeding Risks Both Matter
bottomLine: Active cancer increases recurrent VTE risk, so anticoagulation is generally continued while cancer remains active if bleeding risk is acceptable. Agent choice depends on cancer site, thrombocytopenia, GI or GU bleeding risk, interactions and patient preference.
recognize: Cancer-associated thrombosis may be symptomatic or discovered incidentally on staging imaging.
differentiate: GI or GU cancers and clinically important thrombocytopenia can favour LMWH over a DOAC in selected patients.
assessment: Assess clot burden, bleeding history, platelet count, renal function, cancer site and stage, anticancer-drug interactions and goals of care.
workup: Use standard VTE imaging and baseline CBC and renal function.
management: Use LMWH or an anti-Xa DOAC according to current Thrombosis Canada guidance and individual bleeding risk; reassess duration as cancer activity changes.
medicationSafety: Drug interactions with anticancer therapy and thrombocytopenia can alter anticoagulant choice and dosing.
redFlags: Intracranial tumour with major bleeding risk
counselling: Discuss injection burden, cost and bleeding signs as part of shared treatment choice.
followUp: Reassess every few months while cancer remains active and again when goals of care change.
examTrap: Choosing a DOAC automatically for every cancer-associated clot without considering GI cancer bleeding risk.
oneLinePearl: Cancer VTE therapy is anticoagulation plus a bleeding-risk and interaction check.
sourceBasis: Thrombosis Canada Cancer and Thrombosis clinical guide

title: VTE Duration: Provoked, Persistent, Recurrent, or Preference-Sensitive?
bottomLine: Anticoagulation duration after VTE depends on provoking factors, persistent risk, recurrence, bleeding risk and patient preferences. A major resolved transient trigger usually supports finite therapy, while active cancer or high-risk persistent thrombophilia often supports continuation.
recognize: Surgery-provoked VTE has lower recurrence risk after treatment than unprovoked or persistent-risk VTE.
differentiate: Not every first unprovoked VTE automatically requires lifelong full-dose anticoagulation; current Canadian guidance emphasizes individualized extended-therapy decisions.
assessment: Classify provoking-factor strength, prior VTE, cancer, thrombophilia, bleeding risk, renal function and patient preference.
workup: Do not order indiscriminate thrombophilia panels when results will not change management.
management: Treat the acute VTE for the required initial period, then use the current Thrombosis Canada recurrence-versus-bleeding framework; reduced-dose DOAC is preferred for many patients who continue extended secondary prevention.
medicationSafety: Reassess major bleeding risk at least periodically when long-term anticoagulation continues.
counselling: Discuss absolute clot-versus-bleeding tradeoffs rather than presenting indefinite therapy as automatic.
followUp: Revisit the decision as comorbidity and patient preference change.
examTrap: Ordering a thrombophilia panel after a clearly surgery-provoked first DVT when the result will not change treatment.
oneLinePearl: Duration is a recurrence-versus-bleeding decision, not a fixed rule for every clot.
sourceBasis: Thrombosis Canada VTE Duration of Treatment clinical guide 2026

title: Cancer Survivorship: Recurrence, Late Effects, and Primary Care
bottomLine: Cancer survivors need ordinary preventive care plus treatment-specific surveillance and late-effect monitoring. More imaging is not automatically better; follow the disease-specific survivorship plan and manage cardiovascular, bone, endocrine, fertility and psychosocial sequelae.
recognize: Late effects depend on prior chemotherapy, immunotherapy, radiation and surgery.
differentiate: New symptoms can represent recurrence, a late effect or an unrelated common disease; avoid diagnostic anchoring.
assessment: Maintain a treatment summary and assess recurrence symptoms, secondary-cancer risk, cardiovascular and metabolic health, bone health, fertility and sexual function and mental health.
workup: Order surveillance only at guideline-supported intervals and investigate new symptoms diagnostically.
management: Coordinate oncology and primary care, vaccination, rehabilitation, lymphedema management and chronic-disease prevention.
medicationSafety: Check prior cardiotoxic or immune-active therapies before attributing new symptoms to ordinary disease.
counselling: Provide a clear survivorship care plan and identify who owns each surveillance task.
followUp: Use risk-based long-term follow-up rather than generic annual whole-body scans.
examTrap: Ordering whole-body imaging routinely for an asymptomatic survivor without a guideline indication.
oneLinePearl: Survivorship care is targeted surveillance plus excellent primary care.
